Taittirīya Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
The Yajurveda is primarily a hand-book of Vedic rituals. It has two branches: the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda and the Śukla Yajurveda. The former is also known as the Taittirīya, and has, like other वेदस्, the Saṁhitā, the ब्राह्मण and the Āraṇyaka sections.
The Taittirīya Upaniṣad comprises the three chapters, 7 to 9, of the Āraṇyaka section. The 10th is the well-known Māhānārāyaṇa or Yājñikī Upaniṣad.
These three chapters are called Śīkṣāvallī, Brahmānandavallī and Bhṛguvallī respectively.
Śīkṣāvallī (12 anuvākas or subsections)
It begins with the oft-repeated and well-known śāntimantra (invocation for peace) śaṁ no mitraḥ.
Then there is a reference to शिक्षा or Śīkṣā, the science of phonetics.
Since the meaning of Vedic mantras is closely dependent on their correct pronunciation and intonation, a knowledge of this science is very necessary.
The Upaniṣad then describes five kinds of meditation, relating the letters of the Vedic mantras to things like पृथ्वी or earth, अग्नि or fire, आचार्य or teacher, माता or मोथेर् and so on. It also gives the special fruits accruing from such meditations.
To achieve anything worthwhile in life, a sound मिन्द् and a sound body are necessary.
Hence, in the next अनुवाक, certain japas of mantras and homas in consecrated fires are prescribed for the benefit of those desirous of wealth, learning, intelligence and wisdom. Towards the end, the teacher of the Vedic गुरुकुल prays that a large number of students come to him for एदुचतिओन्, since it is through them that knowledge and culture will spread in the society later on.
Then is described the meditation on the four vyāhṛtis—bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, suvaḥ and mahaḥ—as identified with the earth, the fire, the sky, the air, the sun, the Vedic mantras, the vital prāṇas in the body and so on, along with their fruits.
The fourth vyāhṛti, mahaḥ, was discovered by the sage Māhācamasya, as identical with ब्रह्मन्/Ātman.
The Vedic metre paṅkti has five lines. A Vedic sacrifice also has five parts. By considering the worlds such as the earth, the deities such as आदित्य, the elemental objects such as water, the vital airs such as प्राण and so on as five-fold (‘pāṅkta’), the contemplation gets elevated to the level of a Vedic sacrifice and results in the meditator getting identified with Hiraṇya-garbha (the World-सोउल्, an aspect of ब्रह्मन्). This is the gist of the seventh अनुवाक.
The next अनुवाक describes meditation on Oṁ in various ways and the fruits thereof.
Even after returning home and settling down as a householder, the Vedic student is expected to continue स्वाध्याय (self study) and pravacana (teaching the वेदस् to worthy students). This helps in preserving and spreading धर्म for the good of the society. This is the main purport of the ninth अनुवाक.
The tenth अनुवाक is a मन्त्र (a sacred text meant for meditation) discovered by (or attributed to) the sage त्रिशङ्कु. It gives a description of the experience of the spiritual oneness with च्रेअतिओन्.
The next अनुवाक, practically the last in this Śīkṣāvallī, contains the famous advice of the आचार्य (Vedic teacher of the गुरुकुल) to a disciple who has completed his training and is about to depart for home. The gist of this (convocation) address may be given as follows:
Speak the truth and follow धर्म in your life. Treat your parents, the teacher and the guests that come to you, as if they are gods. Practise the good and abhor the evil. Imitate only the good conduct even from me. Treat the sagacious ब्राह्मणस् with respect and honour them properly. Give gifts to the needy, considering it as a sacred duty. When in doubt about actions or behaviours seek the guidance of the wise elders. Treat the transgressors of धर्म with a balanced attitude of firmness and kindness. This is the command.
Brahmānandavallī (9 Anuvākas)
This chapter starts with the two well-known शान्तिमन्त्रस् or peace invocations—śaṁ no mitraḥ and saha nāvavatu—as part of the Upaniṣadic text.
‘Brahmavid āpnoti param,’ ‘One who knows ब्रह्मन् attains the Supreme’—this is the primary teaching of this chapter. This ब्रह्मन् is सत्य (truth), ज्ञान (knowledge) and अनन्त (infinite). One who realises it in his own heart, will become omniscient and will get all his desires fulfilled.
Then there is a description of the evolution of this world from the आत्मन् (same as ब्रह्मन्) through the five elements, ड़ोओद् and up to the human being.
In the anuvākas 2 to 5, there is a description of the five types of ātmās or puruṣas (individual beings) called respectively—annamaya, prāṇamaya, manomaya, vijñānamaya and ānandamaya (ātmās or puruṣas). They are actually the five aspects of the jīvātman (the individual Self in bondage) associated with the five kośas or sheaths, viz., the physical body, the vital airs and sense organs, the मिन्द्, the intellect, and अज्ञान (nescience, responsible for bondage and transmigration). One has to transcend them to realise one’s true nature, i.e., ब्रह्मन्/Ātman.
The आत्मन् (or ब्रह्मन्)—according to the sixth anuvāka—created this world out of himself and also entered into it as its inner Self. Hence, all that exists here is he, the आत्मन् or ब्रह्मन्.
Therefore, one who gets established in ब्रह्मन् as his own Self, attains fearlessness. He enjoys bliss since ब्रह्मन् is bliss. This is the main purport of the seventh अनुवाक.
The next अनुवाक describes that all the activities in this created world, like the sun rising or the wind blowing, take place by being strictly regulated by ब्रह्मन्, of whom even the god of death is afraid!
Then there is—in the eighth anuvāka—a very interesting calculation of ब्रह्मा-नन्द (the bliss of attaining ब्रह्मन्) by taking the mānuṣa-आनन्द (ideal happiness of an ideal human being) as the base. According to this, brahmānanda is 1020 (i.e. 1 followed by 20 zeros!) times that of ideal human happiness. In effect it just means that the bliss of attaining ब्रह्मन् is infinite.
The last अनुवाक of this chapter declares how the knower of ब्रह्मन् is freed from all fears and apprehensions. Nor is he subject to regrets and self-condemnation.
Bhṛguvallī (10 anuvākas)
This chapter starts with the request of भृगु-Vāruṇi to his ड़थेर् वरुण to teach him ब्रह्मन्. Stating that ब्रह्मन् is that from which all beings are born, in which they live, and to which they ultimately return, वरुण advises his son to find it out through तपस् (inner peace and concentration of मिन्द्).
Every time भृगु returns, after a brief period of तपस्, with a solution, he is sent back by वरुण, since what he has discovered is only the lower truth. After thus eliminating अन्न (food), प्राण (life-force), मनस् (mind), and विज्ञान (intellect), he finally arrives at आनन्द (bliss) as ब्रह्मन्, the ultimate cause of the world.
The text then expatiates upon the importance of अन्न or ड़ोओद्. It must not be derided. It should not be refused when offered. It should be increased so that it can be offered to the hungry souls. Similarly when someone asks for shelter, it must not be denied.
This is followed by some more meditations on the internal organs like the hands and feet or the external objects like rain or animals, as ब्रह्मन्, which results in the acquisition of fame or intellectual faculties or even objects of luxury and enjoyment.
The Upaniṣad closes with a beautiful description of a knower of ब्रह्मन् freely roaming about the worlds and bursting with joyous songs.

Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa
------------------------------------------
This is the only ब्राह्मण of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda that is extant now. The entire text along with the svaras (Vedic intonation) has been recovered.
Scholars of Vedic lore are of the opinion that this ब्राह्मण is more ancient than the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa of the Śukla Yajurveda.
This work has 3 kāṇḍas or sections. They are sometimes called aṣṭakas also. Whereas the first two kāṇḍas have 8 prapāṭhakas or chapters each, the last has 12, making a total of 28 prapāṭhakas. The total number of vākyas or prose sentences is 17,480.
The first kāṇḍa deals with the sacrifices like अग्न्याधान, गवामयन, वाजपेय, Somayāgas, Nakṣatreṣṭi and राजसूय. The second kāṇḍa deals with the others like अग्निहोत्र, Sautrāmaṇi, Upahoma, Bṛhaspatisava and Vaiśyasava. The various mantras—mostly from the Ṛgveda—to be used in these rites as also other relevant details are also given.
The third kāṇḍa gives a detailed account of the Nakṣatreṣṭi. Twenty-eight nakṣatras and the mantras to be used for each of them are described.
Other subjects dealt with are: पुरुषमेध, Paśumedha, preparing the यूप (sacrificial post), rectifying the faults in the rites, and अश्वमेध.
Some astronomical details as also the story of the sage Bharadvāja—his vain efforts to learn the whole of the Veda which is infinite—find a place.
The very last chapter reflects the teachings of the Vedānta through two symbolic sacrifices: Cāturhotra and Vaiśvasṛja. It is total renunciation that leads to लिबेरतिओन्.
Now, a few words about the condition of the society as reflected in this work. वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् were extremely common. Cows were the main items of gifts, especially during the sacrifices, along with gold and cloth. Naturally, agriculture and dairy farming got the pride of place. The वर्ण system was firmly established. अश्वमेध sacrifice was quite common among the kings and emperors. Kṣattriyas used to gather in large numbers for राजसूय sacrifices. Women had an honourable place. Discussions on subjects pertaining to the sacrifices and philosophical topics used to be held, often during the sacrifices. The origins of the stories of the later पुराणस् could be found in these discussions.
On the whole this is an interesting ब्राह्मण, especially to get an idea of the details of the वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् and the society of the times.
See also YAJURVEDA.

Taittirīya Saṁhitā
------------------------------------------
Though 85 शाखास् or recensions of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda are known to have existed, only four have survived to this day. Of these the Taittirīya Saṁhitā is the most important as also the most extensive. Fortunately, all the branches of this Veda—the Saṁhitā, the ब्राह्मण, the Āraṇyaka, the Upaniṣad, the Śrauta and the Gṛhya Sūtras—are available even now.
This Saṁhitā is very well-known and studied in South India. It has 7 kāṇḍas (sections), 44 prapāṭhakas (chapters) and 651 anuvākas (pieces similar to mantras).
In it, the mantras (metrical verses) and prose passages are mixed up. The verses are to be used in वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस्. The prose passages explain how to use them.
The sacrifices dealt with in this Saṁhitā are:
Pauroḍāśa, Yājamāna, वाजपेय, राजसूय, दर्शपूर्णमास and a few Somayāgas.
Sāyaṇa (14th century A. D.) is the most important of the commentators on this Saṁhitā. His commentary is not only extensive but also scholastic.
See also YAJURVEDA.

Taittirīya Āraṇyaka
------------------------------------------
An Āraṇyaka is the third division of Veda.
The Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belongs to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. It has ten prapāṭha-kas or sections. They are also called araṇas and praśnas.
The ten prapāṭhakas are named according to the very first word of each, such as Bhadra, Sahavai, Citti and so on. The prapāṭhakas 7 to 9 form the well-known Taittirīya Upaniṣad. The last is the Mahānārāyaṇa (or the Yājñikī) Upaniṣad.
A very brief summary of the work may now be given:
Prapāṭhaka 1
Details connected with the rite called Āruṇaketuka.
Prapāṭhaka 2
Svādhyāya (study of the वेदस्); pañca-महायज्ञस् (See PAÑCAMAHĀYAJÑAS.)
Prapāṭhaka 3
A symbolic sacrifice called Cātur-hotracitti; importance of the sun as the supporter of the world.
Prapāṭhaka 4
Mantras useful in the प्रवर्ग्य rite (See PRAVARGYA); mantras to be used in अभिचार (black magic).
Prapāṭhaka 5
This section deals mostly with symbols connected with sacrifices.
Prapāṭhaka 6
This deals with mantras used in the पितृमेध (See PITṚMEDHA.).
Some of the special aspects of this Āraṇyaka can now be described:
Methods of knowing, like प्रत्यक्ष and अनुमान; aspects of सूर्य or the Sun-god; विष्णु as the support of the universe; philosophical ideas, similar to the ones in the उपनिषद्स्; some rules about bathing and ड़स्तिन्ग्; असुरस् (nongods or antigods?) too perform sacrifices; meditation on आदित्य or Sun-god; symbolical sacrifices; the Puruṣasūkta; अभिचार or ब्लच्क्-मगिच्.
It is obvious, from a study of its contents, that this Āraṇyaka was not meant only for the vānaprasthins or the forest-dwellers.
